newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Big leaf mahogany fails to gain protection.
newsitem.headline: Big leaf mahogany fails to gain protection.

text.p: A world convention on endangered species rejected a proposal by the United States and Bolivia on Wednesday to list big leaf mahogany, found mostly on the American continent, as an endangered species requiring controlled trade.

Some 67 countries at the 10-day Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) which ends on Friday voted for the proposal, 45 against and nine abstained, failing to muster the two thirds vote it required to pass to the Appendix II list.
Brazil, accused by many environmental pressure groups at the CITES meeting of condoning rising unsustainable mahogany exploitation, was one of those which abstained.
Two leading groups, Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, had actively campaigned for the proposal by Bolivia, as the world's largest mahogany exporter, and the United States, the largest importer.

They argued there was evidence that mahogany is being logged at unsustainable rates and that a large proportion of wood exported is being done in violation of national laws, pointing at a recent audit by Brazil.
Sarah Tyack, a spokeswoman for Friends of the Earth, said CITES's rejection of the proposal showed the abuse of power by the timber industry lobby. "Mahogany is the casualty," she said.

But Jorge Avila, legal adviser to the Bolivia Timber Chamber, dismissed the accusation, saying CITES had simply recognised the "hard facts" and the efforts by different countries to curtail illegal trade.
